note:
Timothy, present at the founding of the Philippian church (Acts 16), is known to the readers (2:22). Elsewhere, Paul calls himself “an apostle” and Timothy “our brother” (2 Cor. 1:1; Col. 1:1).

**servants.** A “servant” is a slave (text note). Timothy is like a son to Paul (2:22), but both are under Christ the Lord. Only here does Paul apply a single title to himself and a “coauthor.” Paul and Timothy’s shared status as slaves reflects the identity assumed by Christ in His incarnation (2:7) (but not His eternal deity and equality with the Father and the Holy Spirit, of course; 2:5–11). Their shared concern for others’ well-being befits their calling (2:20–21).

**in Christ Jesus.** One of Paul’s favorite ways of describing the believer’s union with Christ. This phrase occurs ten times in Philippians.

**overseers and deacons.** These terms designate the twofold leadership in the church at Philippi (1 Tim. 3:1–13) and in all the churches of the NT.

These two words, a concise expression of the effect of Christ’s saving work, appear together in all thirteen of Paul’s salutations. The common source of grace and peace is “God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

Paul’s memory of the Philippians prompts him to pray for them frequently (“in every prayer of mine”) and gratefully (“I thank my God”).

**1:4 with joy.** Joy is a dominant theme in Philippians (vv. 18, 25; 2:2, 17, 18, 28, 29; 3:1; 4:1, 4, 10). See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

The Philippians’ financial support is especially in view (4:10–20).

**in the gospel.** The word “gospel,” Paul’s favorite term for his message, occurs nine times in Philippians (proportionately, more than in any other letter). Paul and the Philippians are bound together by their common commitment to the gospel (v. 7).

**from the first day.** That is, since the gospel first came to Philippi (4:15; Acts 16:12–40).

verse_quote: he ... will bring it to completion.
note: The perseverance of the saints depends upon God’s preserving them by grace. See theological note “Perseverance of the Saints” on p. 1994. God’s “good work” in believers motivates their ongoing effort to “work out” their salvation in the process of sanctification (2:12, 13). God’s saving purpose will be fulfilled on “the day of Christ” (v. 10; 2:16), when He returns in glory to raise His people from the dead (3:11, 20, 21) and to receive universal homage (2:9–11).

The Gk. words could also be rendered “you have me in your heart.” The Philippians are “partakers ... of grace” with Paul through supporting his ministry (cf. v. 5).

**defense and confirmation.** The terms suggest apostolic witness during a trial (cf. v. 16; Mark 13:9–11).
The Gk. noun, like the related verb used often of Jesus in the Gospels (e.g., Matt. 9:36; 14:14), indicates deep emotion.

Paul tells the Philippians not only that he prays for them (v. 4) but also the content of that prayer. Christian belief (“knowledge and all discernment”) comes to expression in Christian love and in behavior that is “pure and blameless” (cf. Col. 1:9–11). The absence of love shows that supposed knowledge is worthless (1 Cor. 13:1–3), and love is itself knowledge of the deepest kind (1 Cor. 8:1–3). The seriousness of Paul’s prayer that “love may abound” among the Philippians will become more apparent in 2:1–18., 10

Not only is the sinner justified through faith in Christ (3:9), but “the fruit of righteousness,” or the righteous life that ensues, is also “through Jesus Christ” through the work of His Spirit (Gal. 5:22, 23), “to the glory and praise of God” the Father. All three persons of the Godhead are active in the sanctification of believers.
Because of Paul’s imprisonment, the gospel has moved irresistibly through the palace guard and beyond.

At the time Paul wrote this epistle, his imprisonment for Christ had become known not only to the soldiers assigned to the emperor, but also to the imperial household (cf. 4:22) and perhaps to the Roman populace beyond.

Paul uses this term to address both men and women (v. 12 text note). Probably both men and women in the church at Rome were involved in communicating the gospel to others, as it seems they were in Philippi (cf. 4:3).

**in the Lord.** This important Pauline phrase points to the believer’s union with Christ and to the divine resources available through Christ to those united with Him (4:13). The phrase occurs nine times in Philippians (counting 2:19). By means of Paul’s imprisonment, the Lord strengthens and encourages the Christians to proclaim the gospel fearlessly.

These are not rival messages, since both parties preach Christ, but opposing motives and attitudes. (Paul reacted with anything but joy when others spread a message other than the gospel of grace in Christ; 3:2, 18, 19; Gal. 1:8, 9). The motive of one group is goodwill and love for Christ, and Paul’s defense of the gospel explains why they love the apostle (vv. 15, 16). The dominant motive of the other group is “rivalry” (v. 15), the very attitude against which Paul warns the Philippians (2:1–5). They preach Christ so that they themselves can seem important, an attitude quite different from Paul’s (vv. 20, 21), and they respond to Paul’s success by seeking to increase his suffering (v. 17).

Paul identifies the third person of the Trinity both as the Spirit of God and as the Spirit of Christ (Rom. 8:9; Gal. 4:6).

**deliverance.** As Paul writes, he expects to be released from prison, but he cannot be certain of that outcome (vv. 20–27; 2:24). He is confident, however, that he will be spared from shame about the gospel at his trial, as God’s Spirit emboldens him to glorify Christ, whatever the legal outcome for Paul before the Roman Empire (v. 20). God will deliver him (v. 28) through His appointed agencies, both human (“your prayers”) and divine (“the Spirit of Jesus Christ”).
Paul’s ultimate goal is neither to live nor to die, but to see Christ magnified regardless of what happens (2:17; cf. Rom. 12:1, 2).

Christ is Paul’s reason for being.

**to die is gain.** Far from severing Paul’s union with Christ, death will bring Paul into a fuller communion with the Christ to whom he is united (v. 23).

Paul wants to be with Christ but also to remain on earth for the sake of the church. This is his dilemma. However, the outcome is in God’s hands, and Paul is confident that God has further work for him to do among the Philippians (vv. 24, 25).

**be with Christ.** Paul’s language here sheds light on the character of the intermediate state (i.e., the condition of a person between the time of his physical death and his bodily resurrection). Paul expects that at his death, he will immediately enter Christ’s presence, which tells us that believers who die before the return of Christ enjoy a spiritual existence in heaven as their souls enjoy the presence of God. At the resurrection, their souls will be reunited with their physical bodies for life in the new heaven and earth (cf. Dan. 12:2; Matt. 22:23–33; 1 Cor. 15:35–49; Rev. 21:1–8). See theological note “Death and the Intermediate State” on previous page.

Paul uses a term that is rare in the NT and has the connotation “conduct as a citizen,” fitting for a colony such as Philippi (see 3:20).

**one spirit ... one mind.** Paul is appealing for unity among the believers. Unity is one important way in which believers’ lives are shown to be “worthy of the gospel of Christ.” “One spirit [or Spirit]” may refer to the Holy Spirit (Eph. 4:3, 4). Paul’s exhortation at 2:1, 2 mentions God’s Spirit and the oneness of mind among believers that He effects.

**striving.** Paul urges his readers not to break under the pressure of opposition, but instead to exert pressure of their own. This means proclaiming the gospel they have believed (Eph. 1:13) and living in a manner worthy of it. The military/athletic associations of this term would resonate with the large number of retired Roman troops in Philippi. It recurs at 4:3, though there the ESV renders it “labored side by side.”

Paul offers the Philippian believers four assurances. (1) Their courage in the face of opposition is a sign of the divine judgment facing the persecutors (2 Thess. 1:5–10). (2) Their courage is also a sign of the believers’ own salvation in its fullest, redemptive sense (Rom. 1:16; 13:11). (3) Suffering for Christ is an honor given by God (3:10). (4) Paul shares in their struggle (vv. 7–26; Acts 16:19–24; 1 Thess. 2:2), and his example can encourage them just as it does “the brothers” (v. 14).

The poetic quality of these verses makes Paul’s words especially forceful. The fourfold appeal of v. 1 (note the repeated word “any”) is the basis for the exhortations of vv. 2–4.

**2:1 encouragement in Christ.** In their union with the Savior, the Philippians find encouragement to pursue unity with one another. To follow Christ’s example, they must first be in Christ (cf. v. 5).

**comfort from love.** Believers are encouraged because Christ loves them (Gal. 2:20) and because they love Christ and one another (v. 2). If Paul’s appeal to unity is here grounded here in the Trinity, as in Eph. 4:4–6, he may be thinking of the Father’s love (see 2 Cor. 13:14).

**participation in the Spirit.** This phrase may also be rendered “fellowship produced by the Spirit.”

verse_quote: of the same mind ... same love ... full accord ... one mind.
note: The accent on unity is strong (cf. 1:27).

Pride is competitive by nature and tries to lift a person above others, so it divides and promotes conflicts rather than harmony (vv. 2, 14; 1:27). By contrast, humility accepts a place of service, with concern for the needs and interests of others (v. 4). Love (v. 2) is essential for humility (1:9; 1 Cor. 13:4, 5).

This verse connects the exhortations (vv. 1–4) to the hymn about Christ (vv. 6–11). Addressing the pride that lies at the root of the Philippians’ discord (1:27–2:4), Paul points to Christ as the supreme example of humility. But Christ is not only an example (Rom. 15:1–3; 2 Cor. 10:1); He is first of all Lord and Savior (v. 11; 3:20).

This “hymn to Christ” may be divided into six stanzas. The first three (vv. 6–8) celebrate Christ’s humiliation, while the last three (vv. 9–11) celebrate His exaltation.

**2:6 in the form of God.** The word “form” refers to the underlying reality and not to appearance only. Jesus’ being in “the form of God” means that He is divine, just as His taking “the form of a servant [slave]” entailed His humbly embracing that identity in His incarnation (v. 7).

**not ... grasped.** This figure of speech means that something desirable was already possessed, but that Christ did not exploit it for personal gain. Unlike Adam in the garden, Jesus was not trying to become God, nor did He capitalize on the privileges that were always His out of self-interest. He does not exercise His deity at the expense of His people; rather, He exercises His divine prerogatives for the benefit of His church.

Christ is not said to have removed from Himself either His deity or His identity as God. Instead, the Son of God added to His person a human nature without surrendering any of His divine attributes. The phrase means that He humbled Himself (v. 8), not relinquishing His divine being but embracing dishonor by becoming human. The nature of His “self-emptying” is defined in three phrases that follow (“taking ... being born . . . being found”). See Introduction: History of Interpretation and theological note “The Humanity of Christ” on p. 2279.

**a servant.** That is, a slave. This language vividly expresses Christ’s willingness to deprive Himself of the enjoyment of the glory befitting His divine status and identity (v. 6 note). Though He continued to possess this glory, even revealing its refulgence to His disciples from time to time (e.g., Matt. 17:1–8), He veiled it in human flesh during His earthly ministry in order to save His people from their sin.

**the likeness of men.** Christ is truly human. “Likeness” means more than similarity. In order to die (v. 8), He had to be completely human. At the same time, Paul makes one important distinction between Christ and other human beings. Unlike them, He has no sin (2 Cor. 5:21; cf. Rom. 8:3). And regarding His divine nature, He remains transcendent over created reality; He cannot and did not cease to be a divine person with a divine nature even in His humiliation.

Christ’s appearance as a man was not an illusion. He revealed Himself through a complete and genuine human nature united with His divine nature in one divine person. He possesses all the essential attributes of humanity, though unlike us, He has never sinned (cf. v. 7 notes; 1 Pet. 2:21–25).

**he humbled himself.** The language here is parallel to the phrase “emptied himself” in v. 7. Each act occurs by the free exercise of Christ’s own will.

**obedient.** Submission to the Father’s will (Heb. 10:5–9) is more significant for the One who is equal with the Father (v. 6) than for anyone else. Paul’s words embrace Christ’s whole lifetime of obedience, while emphasizing that the supreme expression of obedience was His death.

**a cross.** The accent at this point is on Christ’s willingness to suffer the most shameful of deaths, rather than on the atoning significance of the event (cf. Rom. 3:21–26).

The Father’s act is a direct response to Christ’s obedience (Acts 2:24, 32–36).

**highly exalted him.** Christ is restored to the glorious status He had at the beginning but voluntarily chose not to exercise for a time in order to become a human servant (John 16:28; Heb. 2:9, 14).

**the name that is above every name.** This is the “name”—that is, the title—“Lord,” conferred on the Jesus the Messiah in His exaltation in recognition of His complete obedience in His redemptive mission from the Father (Acts 2:36; Eph. 1:21). The God-man is shown to be more than worthy to be called Lord because He successfully accomplished His mission to bring salvation, and so His humanity shares in the glory and honor that He is due.

This may mean “the name belonging to Jesus,” i.e., “Lord” (v. 11). Paul likely means that the revelation of Jesus as the “Lord” is the signal that “every knee should bow” to offer Him worship and that every tongue should acclaim Him Lord. Paul alludes to Is. 45:14–25, where the bowing of every knee and the confession of every tongue (Is. 45:23) are directed toward Israel’s covenant Sovereign, the Lord (Yahweh), who alone is God and alone can save (Is. 45:22).

Christ’s obedient humility resulted in His glory (cf. Matt. 23:12). In the Septuagint, God’s covenant name “Yahweh” is represented by the title “Lord” (Gk. _kyrios_), which appears in English translations as “LORD.” Jesus is now identified with the Lord of Isaiah. At the consummation of Isaiah’s prophesied restoration of Israel in Is. 45:23–25 (fulfilled in the church, which by union with Christ is true Israel), at the very end of time, all will subject themselves to Jesus, since He is the divine and sovereign Lord. Christ is now acclaimed to be what He has always been, the true God (1 John 5:20), and is therefore worshiped as such. The ascription of praise embraces both the humanity (“Jesus”) and the deity (“Lord”) of Christ; He is acknowledged to be the exalted and enthroned God-man. See theological note “The Deity of Christ” on p. 1851.

**God the Father.** Jesus Christ is the Son of the Father. So united are the persons of the Godhead that the act of worshiping the Son glorifies the Father. Although he does so elsewhere (Rom. 8:3; Gal. 4:4), in Philippians Paul does not refer to Jesus as the Son of God explicitly.

On the basis of Christ’s supreme example, Paul resumes his appeal. The apostle’s presence encourages the Philippians to obey, but the basic motivation is from “God who works” in them (v. 13), and their obedience will flourish in Paul’s absence as well (1:27).

**your own salvation.** As in 1:28, this is salvation in the fullest, redemptive sense with particular stress on the sanctification of the believer. The sanctifying process calls for obedience to the exhortation of vv. 1–5. See theological note “The Holy Spirit as Sanctifier” on p. 2023.

**fear and trembling.** This is awe and reverence rather than panic and alarm. The right emotions are stirred by the presence of God (v. 13), and not by misgivings or despair about one’s standing in Christ.

The use of human effort (v. 12), far from violating God’s will, is just what He commands for achieving His sanctifying purpose (Eph. 2:8–10). Moreover, the internal, transformative work that His Spirit has begun (1:6) gives hope that believers’ efforts to die to sin and live to righteousness will bear fruit. Having invoked the example of Christ, Paul reassures the Philippians that they do not will and work on their own, but their wills and their actions are the very arenas where God’s own power is working (4:13; 1 Thess. 2:13).

The Philippians must not imitate the ancient Israelites (Ex. 15:24; 16:7–9; 1 Cor. 10:10). Note also the allusions in v. 15 to Deut. 32:5: unlike God’s ancient people, believers in Jesus are indeed God’s “children,” not “a crooked and twisted generation.” Amid their sufferings from external opponents (1:28–30), the Philippians may have grumbled against church leaders (greeted personally in 1:1) as the Israelites did against Moses (v. 29; 1 Thess. 5:12, 13).

The corporate witness of a united church is in view.

**blameless and innocent ... without blemish.** The meanings of these terms overlap considerably. Paul describes the quality of life required of “children of God.” Such persons will “shine as lights in the world,” in marked contrast to their “crooked and twisted” contemporaries, but offering hope to them at the same time (cf. Matt. 5:14–16; Acts 2:40).

Paul is concerned with the Philippians’ own fidelity to the gospel of Jesus Christ (1:27; 2:1–5).

**the word of life.** This refers to the gospel as a declaration of the saving significance of Jesus’ death and resurrection, and to the life-promoting ethical teachings founded on the saving work of Christ. (1:27; 4:8, 9).

**I may be proud.** Paul’s pride on the “day of Christ” (1:10; cf. 1:6) will be the Philippians’ spiritual growth rather than his own (1:9–11).

verse_quote: if I am to be poured out.
note:
Paul here refers not to his present suffering, but to the possibility that he will die as a martyr. During a later imprisonment, he invokes the same image to express his expectation of imminent martyrdom (2 Tim. 4:6).

**drink offering.** A libation normally of wine, not blood, that accompanied sacrifices (Num. 28:7, 8).

**sacrificial offering of your faith.** Elsewhere, Paul describes the Philippians’ gifts to him as a fragrant offering and a sacrifice pleasing to God (4:10–20). Here, Paul seems to envision the Philippians’ whole lives (Rom. 12:1; 15:16), offered in grateful consecration, as the sacrifice that his own martyrdom could enhance.

**I am glad and rejoice.** For Paul, suffering can cause joy to flourish. It is to be the same for the Philippians (v. 18).
This verse echoes the thought of v. 4. Timothy’s life is a model of the selfless, others-serving humility to which Paul calls his readers. It is an image of Christ’s own humility (vv. 5–11).

verse_quote: as a son with a father.
note: Paul emphasizes that Timothy has worked closely with him for Christ; both are servants of Christ (1:1). As Christ’s servant, Timothy “will be genuinely concerned” for the welfare of others (v. 20). And as Paul’s spiritual “son” (1 Tim. 1:2), Timothy will reflect to the Philippians, when he arrives, the compassion of Paul, his “father.”

Amid difficult circumstances (1:29, 30), perhaps including a forthcoming trial, Paul needs a person of Timothy’s character. Moreover, if Paul waits to send Timothy until the verdict is rendered, Timothy can carry this news to Philippi immediately—soon to be followed, Paul expects, by the apostle himself (repeating the confidence expressed in 1:19–26).
The plans concerning both Timothy and Paul are submitted to the divine will (v. 19; see Rom. 1:10).

This fellow worker of Paul, like Timothy, is worthy of honor. Like Timothy and like Jesus Himself, he is a man for others. He obeys Christ by enlisting as a servant to other believers, both the Philippians (4:18) and Paul, for whose sake he risks his life (vv. 26, 27, 30).

**your messenger and minister to my needs.** As a member, perhaps a leader (v. 29), of the Philippian church, Epaphroditus had carried the congregation’s financial donation to Paul (4:18) and stayed on to serve in other ways, despite his brush with death through a life-threatening illness (vv. 27, 30).
Such is the attitude of Epaphroditus that he is less concerned about his sickness than about the effect of this news on the Philippians.

verse_quote: the more eager to send him.
note: Although Timothy’s departure for Philippi will await the resolution of Paul’s legal appeal, Paul is dispatching Epaphroditus immediately, probably bearing this epistle, to reassure the Philippians’ concerns over Epaphroditus’s health and Paul’s situation, to express thanks for the gift Epaphroditus had brought, and to address other pastoral concerns.

This anticipates the letter’s closing exhortations (4:2–9), but also places the Philippians’ joy in their anticipated reunion with Epaphroditus (2:29) in the context of the deepest source of joy, their relationship to “the Lord.”

**rejoice in the Lord.** This appeal is repeated in 4:4.

**the same things.** This refers to what Paul is about to say in vv. 2–21 (cf. v. 18). Here Paul repeats material he had previously communicated, either personally or by letter, that the Philippians might be “safe” against false teaching in the church.

Paul’s opponents here may be either non-Christians or Christians (as in Galatians) who champion the law of Moses and insist on circumcision as the badge of salvation (cf. Acts 15:1). Although Philippi had so small a Jewish population that it had no synagogue, the reaction against the gospel from many Jews in nearby Thessalonica (Acts 17:5–9) may help to explain why traveling Judaizers now posed a threat to this church composed of Gentiles with a pagan past. First-century Jews considered dogs to be unclean animals. The term “mutilate” is a play on the Gk. word “circumcision.” It is associated with pagan rites of self-inflicted torture (Lev. 21:5; 1 Kin. 18:28). By describing his opponents this way, Paul stresses that they are true neither to the law of Moses, rightly understood, nor to the gospel that Paul preached.

In response to the Judaizers and their mistaken emphasis upon the external physical rite of circumcision, Paul asserts that Christians are the true circumcision, i.e., the true spiritual Israel (Gal. 3:6–4:7). He has OT precedent (Deut. 10:16; 30:6) for emphasizing that heart-transformation by God’s Spirit, not merely a physical incision, reveals the true significance of circumcision. Rom. 2:25–29 also makes the point that true circumcision is of the heart and that Gentiles can possess such a spiritual circumcision, which is another way of referring to them as the authentic Israel.

**glory in Christ Jesus.** This stands in stark contrast to “confidence in the flesh.”

**flesh.** As used by Paul, this term often embraces our humanity insofar as it is in rebellion against God. In this verse, the physical act of circumcision is included (v. 5; Gal. 6:12–15) as representative of the entire list of human advantages and attainments on which Paul himself once rested his confidence for God’s favor (vv. 4–6).
These verses list Paul’s sevenfold pedigree under the law.

Paul was circumcised in accordance with Gen. 17:12.

**of Israel.** See Rom. 9:3, 4; 11:1.

**of the tribe of Benjamin.** Paul (Saul) may have been named for King Saul, also from Benjamin (1 Sam. 9:1, 2). After the division of Israel into northern and southern kingdoms, Benjamin along with Judah remained loyal to the dynasty of David (1 Kin. 12:21).

**a Pharisee.** Paul’s life was one of scrupulous obedience to the law, both the Torah and associated Jewish traditions (Acts 22:3; 26:5; Gal. 1:14).

See Acts 9:13, 14; 22:4, 5; 26:9–11; 1 Cor. 15:9; Gal. 1:13, 14. Although tragically misguided, Paul’s persecution of Christ’s people did express a zeal for God’s glory (see Rom. 10:2).

**blameless.** This is not a claim of sinlessness (Rom. 7:7–13), but of general fidelity to the OT’s prescribed way of life (cf. Luke 1:6). Paul’s outward obedience to the law was honorable (including the offering of prescribed sacrifices for inadvertent transgressions); but his resulting “confidence” (the word is repeated three times in vv. 3 and 4) was the worst of sins.

Paul is obviously not thinking of his transgressions of the law but of his scrupulous obedience to its commands (v. 6).

**I counted as loss.** This decision is the more meaningful, because it is (at least in part) a virtue that he renounces, making it perhaps even harder than renouncing vice. Yet as Paul now grasps, the nobler one’s lineage and the higher one’s attainments, the greater the temptation to pride and self-confidence (Luke 18:9–14; Eph. 2:8, 9). Paul freely discards all sources of self-confidence and personal profit for Christ.

The Gk. word is graphic; it means “refuse” and was once translated “dung.” It refers to that which is not only repulsive to people but also ceremonially defiling before God (Deut. 23:12–14). Paul flings away in disgust whatever interferes with “the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord.”

Verse 9 speaks of justification, v. 10 of sanctification, and v. 11 of glorification.

**3:9 not having a righteousness of my own.** Paul now recognizes that justification is based not upon human attainments of obedience to the law, but entirely and exclusively upon “the righteousness from God,” the merits of Christ given to those united with Christ (Rom. 1:16, 17; 3:21–26).

**faith in Christ.** Christ is the object of faith (Gal. 2:16), and now that he trusts Christ alone, Paul abandons all reliance on his own credentials (vv. 7, 8). Faith is the instrument, not the ground, of justification, and Paul declares justification is “through faith,” never “on account of faith.” The ground of justification is the merit of Christ. Faith as the instrument does not provide value of its own but links believers to Christ and His merit. Moreover, faith is the only instrument of justification; by faith alone in Christ alone we are declared righteous in Christ, and our works play no part in this (cf. Rom. 3:21–4:25).

**depends on faith.** Faith receives God’s gift of righteousness (Rom. 3:22; 5:17), and on the ground of this righteousness, the verdict of justification is given when a person believes (Rom. 4:3; 5:1; Gal. 3:6). In this way, faith and justification occur at the same time, although faith is logically first. See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

This is Paul’s most passionate longing (1:20–23); he speaks not merely of greater mental awareness, but of deepened personal union. The following two clauses explain how knowing Christ is presently experienced.

**his resurrection.** For Paul, identification with the crucified and risen Christ is fundamental to Christian living. Elsewhere (2 Cor. 4:7, 10, 11), Paul teaches that it is through participation in the sufferings of Christ that the power of Christ’s resurrection is manifested in the life of the Christian. This identification with the sufferings of Christ is not exclusively in martyrdom (2:17) but for all of life (Rom. 8:17).

Paul recognizes that the believer’s perseverance depends on the will and the working of the sovereign God (1:6; 2:13; 3:12–14, 21; cf. Heb. 6:3). His present circumstance and Epaph­roditus’s recent crisis show him that the route to resurrection that God has ordained for believers may include death by martyrdom (1:20–21), disease (2:26–30), or some other means.

**the resurrection.** Sharing in Christ’s suffering prepares us for sharing in His glory at the resurrection from the dead (vv. 20, 21; Rom. 8:17).

verse_quote: Not that I have already obtained.
note: The prize of salvation in its fullness has not yet been won, a point Paul emphasizes against ideas of perfectionism (cf. 1 Cor. 4:8; 2 Tim. 2:18; 1 John 1:8). Believers do not yet fully experience all of the benefits of redemption, for we await our glorification, at which point the Lord will remove the presence of sin. Yet the saving process that will be consummated on the day of Christ (1:6, 10) and the resurrection from the dead (3:11) has already begun. Therefore, Paul has said, believers presently experience the resurrection power of Christ (3:10, 11). This salvation will surely be consummated for all who have put their faith in Christ alone (1:6; cf. Rom. 8:28–30).

The objective of Paul’s striving promises a splendid trophy—salvation in all its fullness (cf. 1:28; Rom. 13:11). As in his correspondence with Corinth in Achaia to the south (1 Cor. 9:24–27; cf. 1 Tim. 4:7–10), Paul invokes the athletic imagery of the Panhellenic Games to characterize the purposeful striving involved in Christian perseverance in faith.

**the upward call of God.** God has already called Paul (Gal. 1:15; cf. Rom. 8:30). It is because “Christ Jesus has made [Paul] his own” (v. 12) that he presses forward toward the goal of life in glory (v. 13).

verse_quote: those of us who are mature.
note:
These words may be a tribute to people who in fact think and live maturely. Another possibility is that here Paul is speaking ironically to people who consider themselves already “perfect” (v. 12), and whose thinking Paul needs to correct by showing them that true “maturity” or “perfection” in this life consists in recognizing that one is far from perfect, as true perfection is measured by Christ’s complete perfection (Eph. 4:13).

**think this way.** This refers to Paul’s humble mind-set and ongoing pursuit as expressed in vv. 12–14.

**if ... you think otherwise.** These words may reinforce the preceding appeal to agree with Paul, but the repeated phrases (“think this way ... think”) recall 2:1–5 and suggest that the apostle is also concerned that the Philippians agree among themselves.

**God will reveal.** Whether spiritual discernment and understanding or agreement among believers is in view, the grace of God is necessary (1:9–11). In the meantime, believers’ conduct should accord with the degree of insight that God has already granted (v. 16).

Paul’s example and that of his colleagues, whose “walk” reflects his, are the opposite of what follows in vv. 18, 19. Paul is faithful to the cross (Gal. 6:14), Christ is his glory (v. 21; cf. v. 3), and his mind is set on heavenly things (vv. 20, 21).

These verses could describe all sorts of opponents (1 Cor. 1:23), including Judaizers (vv. 2–6; Gal. 2:15–21). Paul may be thinking especially of people who consider themselves to be living on an exalted spiritual plane, which frees them to enjoy sensual pleasures, whether food (“their god is their belly”) or sex (“they glory in their shame”; cf. 1 Cor. 6:9, 10).

**3:18 with tears.** Paul weeps, not because he fears someone can undo what Christ has done, but because of the destruction in store for opponents of the gospel. This destiny (v. 19) completes the destructive process initiated by their own sin (Rom. 1:18–32; Gal. 6:7, 8). Paul’s confidence that God’s sovereign decision distinguishes those who will receive His grace from those who remain under His wrath never hardened his heart or lessened his compassion toward those outside of Christ (Rom. 9:1–3)., 19

Just as Philippi was a Roman colony (Acts 16:12), the church is a colony of heaven. Although presently at a great distance, physically speaking, from the heavenly “city” where the redeemed can see the Lord reigning over all creation in glory, the followers of Jesus already belong to that city, which defines their identity and eternal privileges.

**we await.** This anticipation is a counterpart to the longing of 1:23. All other instances of this verb in Paul’s epistles have a similar focus (Rom. 8:19, 23, 25; 1 Cor. 1:7; Gal. 5:5).

In the face of opponents’ sinful misuses of the human body (vv. 18, 19 note), Paul celebrates Christ’s transformation of our bodies in conformity with His glorious body (cf. 1 Cor. 15:50–53). See theological note “The Last Resurrection” on p. 2040.

**like his glorious body.** Christ Himself rose bodily from the grave, the “firstfruits” of a great harvest (1 Cor. 15:20–23). As the Father thus vindicated Christ’s obedience (2:6–11), Christ’s resurrection assures believers, united to Him in His death and resurrection, of the glorious resurrection prepared for them.

**subject all things.** See 1 Cor. 15:20–28.

Paul may be anticipating the exhortations that follow, especially the difficult ones of vv. 2 and 3. This helps to explain the presence of so many terms of affection in v. 1. The challenge to “stand firm” recalls 1:27 (where the same command occurs), and “labored side by side” in Paul’s description of Euodia and Syntyche (v. 2) represents a term with military overtones that also appeared in 1:27 (“striving side by side”). The summons to steadfast unity rests immediately upon the declaration of hope in 3:20, 21. Paul is thinking of Christ’s return when he calls his readers a “joy” and “crown” (1 Thess. 2:19, 20).

Paul pleads rather than commands, and by addressing each woman in turn and by name he strengthens his tender appeal.

**Euodia ... Syntyche.** These women are mentioned only here in the NT. They are courageous Christian servants and apparently people of influence in the first-century church.

**agree.** Paul’s main concern is not that they should agree with each other, as is sometimes suggested, but that they should both have the attitude commended in 2:2, a oneness of affection and purpose that gladly honors the other.

Presumably, the Philippians knew the individual whom Paul enlisted to aid the reconciliation of these treasured sisters in Christ, and he was probably among the overseers greeted in 1:1. See text note for alternative interpretations of the Gk. word (_syzygos_). It may be a proper name, or it may metaphorically express Paul’s appreciation for a fellow leader who “pulls the plow” in sync with the apostle, as two well-matched oxen do when “yoked together” (the origin of _syzygos_; cf. 2 Cor. 6:14).

**with Clement.** The name occurs only here in the NT.

**book of life.** The names of all God’s elect are inscribed in this book (Rev. 3:5; 20:15; cf. Ex. 32:32).

The theme of joy is prominent in Philippians. The command to rejoice can always be obeyed, even in the midst of conflict, adversity, and deprivation, because joy rests not on favorable circumstances, but “in the Lord.” Paul uses repetition to emphasize this truth.

The Gk. word denotes the generous spirit that rises above offenses, or a forbearing spirit, of which Jesus provides the supreme example (2 Cor. 10:1). Such a person does not insist on his rights (2:1–4). Only such people learn the secret of joy.

**The Lord is at hand.** This may be understood temporally, looking to Christ’s coming as a future event (3:20, 21), and taking hope from this. Or Paul may also be speaking of Christ’s abiding presence with those united to Him (1:1), perhaps alluding to Ps. 145:18, which promises the Lord’s nearness to those who call on Him (since Paul is about to call readers to pray instead of worrying). Similar expressions in James 5:8, 9 and 1 Pet. 4:7 favor the temporal interpretation.

verse_quote: do not be anxious about anything.
note:
Although the same word is used in 2:20 of a loving concern for others, here it denotes an anxiety that is incompatible with trust in God. Compare Jesus’ arguments against unbelieving anxiety in the Sermon on the Mount (Matt. 6:25–34).

**in everything.** Paul’s language is deliberately all-inclusive; there are no restrictions on applying it.

**prayer and supplication with thanksgiving ... requests.** The four terms used here make up two couplets. Paul is not defining separate types of prayers; rather, the cluster of words shows what importance he attaches to the practice of prayer. Presenting requests in prayer provides an outlet for anxiety (1 Pet. 5:7). Doing so “with thanksgiving” is itself an antidote to worry.

This is the Lord’s direct answer to the prayer that replaces and counteracts anxiety. Things that cannot be fully comprehended can nonetheless be peacefully experienced by those who are “in Christ” (1:1; cf. Eph. 3:18, 19). God’s peace is especially inexplicable when it “guards” (a military image meaning “to take into protective custody”) believers’ hearts in the midst of threatening circumstances, such as Paul’s present imprisonment and his recent deprivation before the Philippians’ gift arrived (vv. 10–19).

Concluding these exhortations, Paul calls his readers to a life of obedience, the right response to the peace of God. The virtues listed are not exhaustive but representative, and they come to expression in countless ways (note the repeated “whatever”). Thinking on such things is not an end in itself, but preparation for purposeful action (v. 9).

**true.** See Eph. 4:24, 25.

**honorable.** The Gk. word means “worthy of respect.”

**just.** See Titus 1:8.

**pure.** See 1 Tim. 5:22.

**lovely ... commendable.** Terms used only here in the NT.

The Philippians are to be guided both by Paul’s teaching and by his example, especially his love for the Philippians (v. 1; 1:3–8; 2:12) but also his response to suffering (1:12–30) and his ongoing pursuit of Christlike holiness (3:12–17).

**the God of peace.** Paul inverts his earlier assurance that “the peace of God” would protect the praying Christian’s heart from anxiety (v. 7). Here he points to an even greater promise: God does not send His peace from afar, remaining aloof in heaven; rather, the Holy Spirit, who is God Himself, comes near to deliver His peace (cf. John 14:16–18, 26, 27).

Paul returns to a theme of ch. 1—the Philippians’ partnership in the gospel (1:5), especially their financial support. He acknowledges their recent gift with thanks while setting before them the example of his own contentment through a range of financial ebbs and flows.

**4:10 you had no opportunity.** Paul adds a qualification, lest they think he is rebuking them.

These verses do not deny the reality of Paul’s need, but rather testify that he is content to live both in plenty and in want.

**4:11 content.** In first-century Stoicism, “contentment” was an admired virtue, the trait of true wisdom. But Stoic “contentment” was self-sufficiency, grounded in aloof indifference. Paul’s contentment was utterly reliant not on himself and his ability to suppress emotions, but on Christ, who held Paul fast and sustained him in all circumstances.

Relying on Christ’s power (1:19; 2:12, 13) and following His example (2:5; 3:10), Paul is able to face all circumstances with contentment. He wants to impress the same lesson upon his readers (vv. 6, 7, 19).
The qualifications of vv. 10–13 call for the restatement of Paul’s gratitude for their assistance to him in his time of real need (1:17).

Even before Paul left Macedonia, the Philippians were repeatedly generous to him.

**4:15 in the beginning of the gospel.** That is, upon the arrival of the gospel in Philippi (1:5).

**when I left.** Paul left Macedonia to go to Achaia during his second missionary journey (Acts 16:40–18:18). In 2 Cor. 11:9, Paul mentions receiving gifts from Macedonian churches such as Philippi while he ministered in Corinth. It appears that these gifts, delivered by Silas and Timothy, freed Paul from supporting his team through his tent-making to be able to devote more time to spreading God’s Word (Acts 18:5).

As is made emphatically clear in v. 18, Paul is amply supplied and wants to place no further strain on the church’s resources. Yet the main cause of Paul’s rejoicing (v. 10) is not that his needs have been fully met. Rather, he perceives that the Philippians’ gifts are an act of worship pleasing to God (Heb. 13:15, 16), and he knows that God will richly bless them in return (2 Cor. 9:6).
This refers to both material and spiritual needs (vv. 6, 7). The promise is for those who are in Christ Jesus (v. 21; 1:1).

This recalls 1:1. Paul embraces every Philippian believer with his affection and greeting to imply once more that they must put aside their self-interests and grow in the love (1:9–11) and humility that will preserve and deepen their unity in Christ (2:1–4).

**brothers.** Here, as elsewhere, fellow believers of both sexes. Paul frequently addresses the Philippians with this term (1:12; 3:1, 13, 17; 4:1, 8).

**who are with me.** See 1:1, 14.

This points to the corporate unity of believers, whether within a single congregation or among local churches, such as the churches in Philippi and Rome.

**Caesar’s household.** Probably not members of the emperor’s family but servants in the palace. These would be the Roman believers with whom Paul has most contact (1:13).
